Merge sort — guided tour

plan.contextChunk: This figure traces the operation of merge sort on an eight-element array as a bottom-up lattice of gray boxes linked by thick gray arrows. The bottom rank, tagged "initial sequence", holds eight single-element squares reading 5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6 from left to right. Pairs of arrows, each pair captioned "merge", lift adjacent squares into four two-element boxes reading 2 5, 4 7, 1 3, and 2 6. A second rank of merge arrows combines those into two four-element boxes, 2 4 5 7 and 1 2 3 6. A last pair of arrows, again captioned "merge", brings both into the wide box at the top, tagged "sorted sequence", which reads 1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7. Box width scales with the run it holds, so the doubling of sorted-run length shows up directly as the boxes widen from rank to rank while their count halves. Read upward, the drawing presents the algorithm as repeated merging of already-sorted runs.

interactionPlan.concept: Merge sort builds a sorted array bottom-up by repeatedly merging two already-sorted runs, doubling run length and halving run count at every level of the recursion tree.
elements: Top caption label 'sorted sequence'
Top-rank wide gray box containing 1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7 (the final merged run)
Rank-2 gray box (left) containing 2 4 5 7
Rank-2 gray box (right) containing 1 2 3 6
Bottom rank of eight small single-element squares: 5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6 left to right
Bottom caption label 'initial sequence'
Thick gray arrows in pairs pointing upward from each pair of child boxes to its parent box (14 arrows total)
Text label 'merge' centered between each arrow pair (7 labels: four at the lowest rank, two at the middle rank, one at the top)
Box width scaling: box width proportional to number of elements it holds
Highlight overlay: active source pair, active arrow pair, and active destination box (used during stepping)
Cursor markers (small triangles) under the front element of each source run during a merge
Output staging strip inside the active destination box showing values appended so far, with empty slots for the rest
Comparison readout annotation, e.g. 'front(left)=2  vs  front(right)=1  →  take right'
Optional color tint on the two duplicate value-2 elements (one from the left half, one from the right half) for the stability trace
Small legend: gray = sorted run, highlighted outline = active merge, tinted = tracked duplicate keys

interactions.teaches: That merging two sorted runs is a single linear scan driven by one comparison of the two front elements, and that the tie-breaking rule in that comparison is exactly what makes merge sort stable.
interactions.label: Implement merge(left, right) for the highlighted pair

api.does: how many elements of that run have not been consumed yet
peek at the value under that run's cursor — read only, consumes nothing
true when front(a) <= front(b); the tie case (<=) is what preserves original order
pop that run's front element and append it to the output box — the ONLY way to move a value
attach your own comment to the current frame of the replay

interactions.frame: both source runs with their cursors, the partially filled output box, and the 1-2 elements the op just compared or moved
interactions.success_check: The output box holds every element of both runs, is non-decreasing left to right, and equal keys appear in left-run-before-right-run order (the tinted 2 from the left half precedes the tinted 2 from the right half).

interactions.teaches: That each level of the tree doubles the length of the sorted runs and halves their count, so only log n levels of merging are needed.
interactions.label: Merge-sort level

interactions.teaches: That stability is a property of the comparison inside merge, not of the final sorted values — the two equal 2s are distinguishable and keep their original relative order.
interactions.label: Track duplicate 2s (stability trace)

demo_steps.title: Eight one-element runs
demo_steps.narration: The bottom rank shows the input 5 2 4 7 1 3 2 6 as eight single-element boxes. A one-element sequence is already sorted, so every one of these is a valid sorted run.

demo_steps.title: First merge pass: runs of 2
demo_steps.narration: Adjacent singletons are merged pairwise into 2 5, 4 7, 1 3 and 2 6. Four merges, each a single comparison — the boxes get twice as wide and half as numerous.

demo_steps.title: Second pass: runs of 4
demo_steps.narration: Two merges combine the pairs into 2 4 5 7 and 1 2 3 6. Watch the cursors: each merge is one left-to-right sweep, never a rescan.

demo_steps.title: Write merge() for the final pair
demo_steps.narration: Now implement merge(left, right) yourself on 2 4 5 7 and 1 2 3 6. Each take() appends one value to the top box, and the replay shows exactly which comparison caused it.

demo_steps.title: Ties and stability
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the duplicate trace: the two 2s are tinted differently. With '<=' the left 2 goes first and order is preserved; swap to strict '<' in the buggy version and the duplicates silently swap places.

demo_steps.title: Sorted sequence
demo_steps.narration: The top box reads 1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7. Three levels of merging over eight elements — log n passes, each touching every element once, giving n log n work.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Merging is cheap because both inputs are already sorted — you only ever compare the two front elements — so the entire cost of merge sort is n comparisons per level times log n levels.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Four ranks stacked bottom-to-top on a white background, all boxes light gray with thin black borders and serif numerals. Bottom rank: eight small equal squares (5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6) evenly spread across the full width, with the caption 'initial sequence' centered below. Third rank: four boxes of double width ('2 5', '4 7', '1 3', '2 6'), each centered above its two children. Second rank: two boxes of quadruple width ('2 4 5 7' on the left, '1 2 3 6' on the right). Top rank: one very wide box '1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7' centered, caption 'sorted sequence' above it. Every parent receives two thick medium-gray arrows angling up-inward from its two children, with the word 'merge' in serif text centered between each arrow pair. Box width should visibly double from rank to rank while box count halves — that geometric relationship is the point of the figure. For the interactive layer: the active merge highlights its two source boxes, its arrow pair, and the destination box with a saturated accent outline (e.g. blue), dims the rest of the tree, and draws small cursor triangles under the front element of each source run; the destination box fills slot by slot as take() fires. When the stability trace is on, tint the 2 originating in the left half one color (e.g. orange) and the 2 originating in the right half another (e.g. teal) and carry those tints all the way up into the final box.

authoredContext: To sort the entire sequence A D hAŒ1; AŒ2; : : : ; AŒni, we make the initial call MERGE-SORT.A; 1; A:length/, where once again A:length D n. Figure 2.4 illustrates the operation of the procedure bottom-up when n is a power of 2. The algorithm consists of merging pairs of 1-item sequences to form sorted sequences of length 2, merging pairs of sequences of length 2 to form sorted sequences of length 4, and so on, until two sequences of length n=2 are merged to form the final sorted sequence of length n.

merge(left, right) workbench API: remaining(run) · front(run) · frontLessEqual(a,b) · take(run) · note(text)

⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Scale/legibility: the tree is drawn into a 900×580 viewbox that is compressed into the narrow left column beside a very wide UI panel, so the box digits (19px in viewbox units) render at roughly 8px — in the source the serif digits are the dominant visual element and are easily read.

Box heights/fills are uniformly thin compared with the source, where all rows (including the singletons) are chunky squares/rectangles with visibly larger padding around the digits; the generated singletons read as tiny chips.

Arrow attachment points differ slightly: in the source the arrows leave the top corners of each child box and land on the parent box's left/right thirds with a long diagonal; the generated arrows are shorter and start nearer the child's centre, making the tree look more compressed vertically.

Extra chrome not in the source (legend swatches, replay caption text at y≈152, cursor triangles, orange/teal duplicate tints) appears in non-default states; the y≈152 replay readout sits only ~11px from the top-level 'merge' label and can visually collide during playback.
evaluation.notes: Topology, mark types, gray palette and all 'merge'/'sorted sequence'/'initial sequence' labels faithfully reproduce the merge-sort tree with an unusually rich and correct set of interactions (level select, demo steps, stability trace, sandboxed merge() workbench with frame replay), but the drawing is squeezed into a small fraction of the width by the oversized control panel, leaving the digits and captions uncomfortably small.
action_items: Shrink the viewbox (or enlarge fonts to ~26–30 units) so box digits and the 'merge' / 'sorted sequence' / 'initial sequence' captions stay legible when the SVG is docked beside the control panel; use setUiLayout to dock the panel below or narrow it so the tree gets most of the width.
Increase box heights and singleton box size with more padding around digits to match the chunkier proportions of the source boxes.
Lengthen the inter-level arrows and anchor them at the child box's outer top corners aiming at the parent's left/right thirds, matching the long diagonals in the source.
Move the replay comparison readout out of the band occupied by the top-level 'merge' label (e.g. below the sorted box or into the UI caption only) to avoid text collisions during playback.
plan_action_items: Rebalance the plan so the code-editor workbench occupies a collapsible secondary panel rather than dominating the layout; the default (step-0) state should read as a drop-in replacement for the static figure at full size.

feedback.rationale: The concept, topology, and interaction set are correct and faithful; the only failures are execution-level scale/layout issues (font sizes, box proportions, arrow anchoring, panel docking, label collision) that can be fixed directly in the rendering code.
